claims.text: Single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticle formation is governed by synchronization of precursor-reduction kinetics.
Concurrent reduction traps the constituent metals in a randomly mixed, high-entropy configuration.
Staggered reduction causes early-formed nuclei to promote phase segregation.
Changing reductant delivery, temperature ramp, or reaction environment can synchronize reduction of all metal precursors.
Low-temperature controlled-atmosphere conditions permit fine tuning of precursor-reduction rates without high-temperature entropy effects.
Synchronized reduction produces uniformly distributed nucleation sites that concurrently incorporate all constituent metals.
Simultaneous reduction and nucleation produce a high density of mixed-metal nuclei.
A high density of mixed-metal nuclei prevents subsequent elemental segregation.
With unsynchronized reduction, early nuclei preferentially incorporate some elements while later-reduced elements deposit separately and form distinct phases.
Conditions engineered for synchronized reduction will yield single-phase, compositionally homogeneous HEA nanoparticles.
An unchanged baseline with kinetic mismatch is more likely to yield multiphase or segregated nanoparticles.
Prior comparable noble-metal bimetallic syntheses produced varied phase outcomes, with phase separation in most tested systems.
The proposed kinetic rule applies to noble-metal systems synthesized by low-temperature or controlled reduction.
The proposed kinetic rule may not apply to high-temperature shock or arc-melting routes because high entropy is then stabilized thermodynamically.
The reduction-timing tolerance required for single-phase formation may depend on precursor chemistry and reaction conditions.
In situ X-ray diffraction can monitor phase evolution in the proposed comparison.
In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy can track the relative reduction kinetics of the constituent metals.
TEM combined with EDX can assess nanoparticle morphology and compositional uniformity.
If deliberately synchronized and deliberately staggered reductions both yield similarly homogeneous single-phase nanoparticles, the proposed governing mechanism is falsified.
A lack of correlation between measured reduction synchrony and phase purity or morphology would falsify the hypothesis.
